answer: Algorithmic Path Diversity Routing enforces sybil resistance by requiring every node to route packets through three independent intermediary clusters before reaching the final destination beacon. To prevent trivial route duplication, the protocol measures edge-disjoint routing tables using an automated network atlas that maps independent upstream routing paths. An attacker launching sybils pays a heavy cost in compute and propagation latency, because fake nodes clustered locally cannot satisfy the strict path-diversity ratios enforced across the wider meadow of interconnected routing domains.
